Therefore T_g im(I-S) is contained in im(I-S), and the group inverse gives equality. With a Hamel basis e_i, ordered tensor coordinates are independent. Images of basis tensors are zero on diagonals and plus/minus the pair differences a_ij=e_i tensor e_j-e_j tensor e_i. Choosing one order i<j gives a basis of A=im(I-S), since the(i,j) coordinate occurs once with coefficient1. Thus a_12 is nonzero in every characteristic, while e_1 tensor e_1 has a nonzero diagonal coordinate and cannot belong to A. This proves universal properness without division by2.
substantive_reconstruction.dimensions_and_characteristic_two: For finite d, unordered distinct pairs count d(d-1)/2 and all ordered pairs count d². Fixed-swap coefficients obey c_ij=c_ji, so a basis of B=ker(S-I) consists of diagonals and off-diagonal sums, giving d(d+1)/2 over every field. Those divisions are integer counts, not field divisions. For d>=2 both A and B are nonzero proper ambient subspaces. When char!=2, Sx=-x identifies A with the negative eigenspace by x=(I-S)(x/2), and the half-projectors split B plus A. In char2, both signed eigenspace equations become Sx=x; they define B, while A is strictly contained in B because it has no diagonal coefficients. original_contract.question: A student asserts: the tensor product of two irreducible representations of a group G is again irreducible. Show this is false by a counterexample. Specifically, take any representation (phi, V) of G with dim V >= 2 (you may take V irreducible) and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V. Exhibit a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V, and compute the dimensions to show V (x) V cannot be irreducible when dim V >= 2.
